text: There is extremely little reason to gain weight faster than you can realistically build muscle, which has a lot of factors outside of just how much food you consume, and is what leads to gaining any body fat during a bulk. If your current bodyfat is above ~17% (for most people,) you probably don't even need to bulk to gain muscle and can do it entirely by recomping or even in a small deficit. For most men, assuming near-perfect conditions, you're looking at being able to gain ~20lb of muscle in the first year of training, ~10lb in year 2, ~5lb in year 3, and so on... It halves every year until it becomes virtually impossible to measure the difference. Unless you are in your first year, you should only be aiming to gain ~1-2lb per month for a solid 8-10 months, then spending the next few months losing any fluff you gained. It could be 10lb, it could be 0lb, just make the call when you get there. The only wrong answer for how quickly to bulk is looking to gain 1lb/week or more unless you are medically underweight. You simply cannot build muscle tissue fast enough to justify gaining weight quickly.

text: A few things: Walking is not cardio in the sense that it will provide meaningful cardiovascular benefits. The effort required to sustain a flat-surface walk at pretty much any pace is simply not challenging enough. If doing basic walks is challening for you (old, injured, disability, etc.) feel free to ignore the rest of this post and just keep on keepin' on. You really need to be doing at least a light jog (pace is mostly irrelevant) or incline walk with a heart rate around 130 to start getting benefits. Another way to gauge it is going at a speed where you can still hold an uncomfortable conversation. You should also be working towards sustaining whatever activity you choose for at least 7-15 minutes to see benefits. The 7000 steps thing is also only relevant for people who do essentially zero other physical activity (typically the elderly, desk jockeys, or otherwise completely sedentary people.) If you don't have a plan, look into starting Couch25K. Since it's time-based you can actually use it on literally any cardio activity (bike, elliptical, stairmaster, swimming... anything.) Intervals are about really cranking your heart rate to create anaerobic adaptations, it's not just going a bit faster or slower, it should be completely unsustainable. This takes some time to build up to, just like any physical endeavour, so if you haven't done incredibly hard sprints that make you feel like you want to puke recently, you'll need an on-ramp by using shorter-than-intended intervals or a slightly slower pace. Typically, you can start with as low as 15 seconds on, 30 seconds off and work your way towards 1 minute on, 2 minute off by adding 5-15 seconds per session. Going longer than 1 minute usually means it's not hard enough. Doing interval work after a different workout is not typically recommended. This shit is suppose to be hard as fuck so you don't want to do it pre-fatigued. There's a reason Intervals only take ~6-10 minutes to do. It is NOT recommended to do intervals on a treadmill, stairmaster, or any piece of equipment that forces you into a fixed pace. Also don't do it in a pool. You should be so gassed that you may need to give up before the interval you're aiming for is actually done, so this is entirely for your own personal safety. I noticed you have Stairmaster in your plan. There is absolutely nothing special about a Stairmaster, or any other specific piece of cardio equipment. You get better at the one you choose to do, but they all result in the same benefits, so don't feel obligated to pick any specific one. Just do what you like to do. I personally do LISS as running and sprints on a row machine. You can do far less Interval work than LISS work. The ratio is not 1:1, but more like 3-4 LISS to 1 Interval for "maximal" benefits.

text: This is an interesting routine that strikes a balance between muscular hypertrophy and cardio vascular conditioning. It excels in that is hits every major muscle group several times a week, in programming a full body work out each session, and through targeting calorically intense motions. It is limited in that it prioritizes exercise over training. This is to say that it would be challenging to progress on some of these lifts in controlled ways. Further, there is an implied artificial distinction between weight loss and muscle growth. In reality, bigger muscles require more energy to maintain. Technically, this may cause you to weigh more (famously muscle is heavier than fat). However, a lb of muscle requires more calories to maintain than a lb of fat. would it be better to do 3 sets? This depends. If you're enjoying yourself, then proceed accordingly. For me, I would at minimum start each session with the leg lifts since legs contain the most muscle and therefore consume the most oxygen. This is a good foundation and you will progress towards your goals if you continue to train regularly, increase either the weight or volume at controlled intervals, replenish your body with nutritious food, and get good sleep. Consider re-evaluating if this stops bringing joy, or if you are unable to increase the volume or weight of your lifts at regular intervals
